name: Honey
short: Honey is linked with infant botulism, so US health authorities advise against it under 12 months. A case report describes anaphylaxis in a child; on wounds it may cause painful discomfort.
text: A review states that numerous studies have linked eating honey with infant botulism, a disease that blocks voluntary muscle and autonomic nerve function, and that honey samples across the United States have tested positive for Clostridium botulinum spores and toxins; on this evidence the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended that honey not be given to infants younger than 12 months. In older children, a systematic review of six randomised trials (899 children aged 12 months to 18 years) of honey for acute cough found that gastrointestinal symptoms were reported more often with honey than with placebo (34 children against 13; risk ratio 1.91, 95% CI 1.12 to 3.24, moderate-certainty evidence; the abstract gives the proportions as 12% and 11%), while nervousness, insomnia and hyperactivity were reported in 9.3% with honey against 2.7% with dextromethorphan, a difference that was not statistically significant; the authors nonetheless concluded overall that adverse events did not differ between the honey and control arms, and most children were treated for one night only. Honey is described as a rare cause of food allergy that can nonetheless cause severe reactions: a case report describes anaphylaxis in a 5-year-old boy sensitised to ragweed and mugwort pollen after he ate artisanal honey. Applied to chronic wounds, a meta-analysis of eight studies (906 people) found that honey dressings may lower the visual analogue scale (VAS) score (the abstract does not say what the scale measured) but may increase the incidence of painful discomfort during treatment, with evidence of very low quality. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
